title: Mahakaccana the explainer
hookLine: the disciple who unfolds short teachings in detail (MN 18)

cards: A man leaning on his walking stick asks the Buddha a blunt question. His name is Dandapani, a Sakyan out for a stroll, and in the Middle Length Discourses he asks: what does the ascetic teach? What does he proclaim?
The Buddha gives a short, strange answer. Dandapani shakes his head, raises his eyebrows, and walks off, still leaning on his stick. That evening the Buddha tells the monks about it.
One monk asks what he meant, and the Buddha answers with another short saying, gets up, and goes inside. And the monks look at each other.

teach.b: Roughly: when a person finds nothing in the world to delight in, to welcome, or to cling to, that is the end of the hidden tendencies of the mind, and the end of taking up sticks and weapons, of quarrels and fights.
Then the Buddha went in. Second, the go-to monk.
The monks remember that the Teacher praised Mahakaccana as able to explain at length what was said in brief. So they go to him.

He chides them, gently: you had the Teacher himself, and you came to me, like someone who wants heartwood and walks past the root and the trunk to search among the branches. Then he unfolds it anyway.
Third, the unfolding. Eye and form meet, and seeing arises. The three together are contact.
With contact comes feeling. What one feels, one perceives. What one perceives, one thinks about.
And what one thinks about, one spins out, on and on, until the spinning comes back and besets the person who started it. That's the road to the quarrels. Fourth, the seal.
The monks take it back to the Buddha, who says: Mahakaccana is wise. If you had asked me, I would have explained it the same way.
Ananda says it's like a hungry, tired man who finds a honey cake: wherever he tastes it, it's sweet.
So the Buddha gives the discourse a name: the Honey Ball.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes take a short saying of the Buddha and explain it at length in a talk, and the Honey Ball discourse is studied for its step-by-step account of how perception turns into proliferating thought.

o: a short riddle with no answer
a walking stick for an elder
a honey ball, a sweet cake

games.q: the honey ball: tap the pairs.
p: asked his question leaning on a stick

s: Mahakaccana refused to explain, since only the Buddha should
he chided the monks gently, then explained it anyway.
the Buddha said he would have explained it the same way
Dandapani stayed and became a monk
he walked off, still leaning on his stick.

games.q: you're one of the monks. the Buddha has said something short and puzzling and gone inside. what do you do?
o: wait until tomorrow and ask him.
go to Mahakaccana and ask him to unfold it.
games.why: they go to Mahakaccana, praised as one who explains at length what was said in brief. he unfolds it, and the Buddha approves every step.

practice: Take one short thing you say often that others don't quite get: a rule at home, a phrase at work, something you know so well you've stopped explaining it.
Walk through it step by step in your mind, the way Mahakaccana did, this, then this, then this, and notice each step you usually skip.

wordCard.voice: Madhupindika, the honey ball. The name given to the discourse where Mahakaccana unfolded the Buddha's short saying step by step. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali madhupindika: a honey cake or honey ball, the name the Buddha gives this discourse.

carryVoice: Your line: unfold it. A short saying can hold a long road. Day seven hundred seventy-five, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 18 (Madhupindika Sutta, the honey ball)
